Succoth (Place)
SUK-uth
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Sukkoth (H5523), "booths, shelters," the plural of sukkah ("booth"). Two places bear the name: a town east of the Jordan where Jacob built booths, and the first Israelite encampment after leaving Egypt.

📖 Biblical Definition

Succoth ("booths") is the name of two distinct places in Scripture. The first is the town east of the Jordan, in the valley near the Jabbok, where Jacob, returning from Padan-aram after his reconciliation with Esau, stopped and built a house for himself and booths (Hebrew sukkoth) for his cattle — from which the place took its name (Gen 33:17). This Succoth in Gilead appears again in the time of the judges, when Gideon, pursuing the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, asked the men of Succoth for bread for his weary troops; they mockingly refused, doubting his victory, and Gideon, after defeating the kings, returned and punished the elders of Succoth with thorns and briers as he had warned (Judg 8:5-16) — a sober lesson on refusing aid to the LORD's servants in the day of battle. The second Succoth was the first station of Israel's journey out of Egypt: after the Passover, "the children of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth" (Exod 12:37; 13:20; Num 33:5-6). This Succoth, on the edge of Egypt, was the first stopping-place of the redeemed nation as they set out toward the wilderness and the promised land. The name "booths" carries forward into the great Feast of Tabernacles (the Feast of Booths, Sukkoth), in which Israel dwelt in booths for seven days to remember that the LORD had made them dwell in booths when He brought them out of Egypt (Lev 23:42-43) — a perpetual reminder that God's people are pilgrims, dwelling in temporary shelters, journeying toward the rest He has prepared. Succoth thus links the patriarch's homecoming, the nation's exodus, and the annual feast of pilgrim-remembrance.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Two places named "booths": the town east of the Jordan where Jacob built booths (Gen 33:17) and where Gideon punished the elders for refusing his troops bread (Judg 8); and the first Israelite encampment after leaving Egypt (Exod 12:37); linked to the Feast of Booths and the pilgrim life.

SUCCOTH (PLACE), proper noun. Hebrew Sukkoth (H5523), "booths, shelters"; the name of two distinct places.

First: the town east of the Jordan near the Jabbok where Jacob built a house and booths for his cattle (Gen 33:17).

There Gideon punished the elders for mockingly refusing bread to his weary troops (Judg 8:5-16).

Second: the first station of the exodus, where Israel journeyed from Rameses after the Passover (Exod 12:37; 13:20; Num 33:5-6).

The name connects to the Feast of Booths (Sukkoth), remembering Israel's pilgrim dwelling in the exodus (Lev 23:42-43).

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 33:17 — "And Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built him an house, and made booths for his cattle: therefore the name of the place is called Succoth."

Exodus 12:37 — "And the children of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand on foot that were men, beside children."

Judges 8:16 — "And he took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth."

Leviticus 23:42-43 — "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days... That your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Succoth is corrupted when its two locations are carelessly confused, when Gideon's punishment of the men of Succoth is read as mere cruelty rather than a lesson on refusing the LORD's servants, or when the pilgrim symbolism of the booths is missed.

expand to see more

Two-Succoths confusion. Scripture names two distinct places Succoth: the town in Gilead east of the Jordan (Jacob, Gideon) and the exodus encampment on the edge of Egypt. They are different locations sharing the common Hebrew word for "booths." Careful reading distinguishes them by context: the Gilead Succoth is associated with Jacob's homecoming and Gideon's campaign; the Egyptian Succoth with the journey out of Egypt. Both, however, share the name's meaning — temporary shelters — and both connect to the pilgrim theme of God's people dwelling in booths.

Succoth has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal points worth recovering are the lesson of Gideon and the men of Succoth, and the pilgrim symbolism of the booths. The men of Succoth refused bread to Gideon's weary troops in the day of battle, doubting the LORD's victory, and were punished for it — a warning against refusing aid and comfort to the LORD's servants when the outcome seems uncertain. And the booths themselves, taken up in the annual Feast of Tabernacles, perpetually remind God's people that they are pilgrims, dwelling in temporary shelters, journeying toward the permanent rest the LORD has prepared (Heb 11:9-10, 13-16). The Christian, too, dwells in a tabernacle that will be dissolved, looking for the building of God, eternal in the heavens (2 Cor 5:1).

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Two places named "booths": the town east of the Jordan where Jacob built booths (Gen 33:17) and Gideon punished the elders (Judg 8); and the first exodus encampment (Exod 12:37); linked to the Feast of Booths and the pilgrim life.
